newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish minister gingers up touchy nuclear debate.
newsitem.headline: Finnish minister gingers up touchy nuclear debate.

text.p: Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto has exposed a weak seam in an otherwise sturdy five-party governing coalition by breaking ranks with his partners on the complex and touchy issue of nuclear power.

At a weekend meeting of his Conservative Party executive, Niinisto suggested parliament could review a freeze on expanding the use of nuclear power -- running counter to a pledge by Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen not to reopen the question during his term to end-1999.

He was not available on Monday to explain his remarks, which came as a committee is reviewing Finland's future energy supply. But they flew in the face of coalition partner the Green league, which is totally against more nuclear power.

While some analysts saw the comments as a bid for political distinction in the colourless consensus of a two-year coalition, others said they may fit a deeper cross-party agenda aimed at keeping Finland on track for Europe's single currency.

Some industrial trade unionists have called for more nuclear power to fuel heavy industry as the best guarantee for competitiveness, investment and jobs in future. They are making job creation a condition for supporting Finland's entry to economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Already at the beginning of the 1980s, we opened this discussion -- that we need more nuclear power to secure electricity for basic industry," Per-Erik Lundh, head of the influential metalworkers' union, told Reuters.
"The higher the price of electricity in Finland goes, the more certain it is that products will be manufactured of Finnish raw materials outside our borders," he told members in a speech.

Social Democrat Lipponen has close ties with all unions, but since taking office in April 1995 has only scratched the surface of unemployment at around 16 percent, despite pledging to halve it to eight to nine percent by 1999.

"We have also to remember the employers' organisations -- they have been most willing to have more nuclear power, and to support the government in going for EMU," said Esko Torsti, economist at Enskilda Banken. "It could be an implicit reward."
He saw a chance that the Greens -- in any case the most junior coalition partner with just one minister in the 18-strong cabinet -- may be sacrificed for broader support.
"It seems to me that (for the Social Democrats) ... it is more important to make sure of the labour unions which have traditional links with the Social Democrats," he said.

Finland's position on the whole nuclear question is very different from neighbouring Sweden, which decided to dismantle its nuclear plants. Finland faces a sharp power shortfall in the near future and potential sources are limited.

Electricity firms say it will need an extra 2,000 megawatts in baseload capacity by 2005 -- the equivalent of more than one nuclear power station or four coal-fired ones, said Anneli Nikula, senior adviser at the Finnish energy industries' federation Finergy.

"We would like to have (the nuclear) option," she said. The alternatives to raise baseload capacity were coal -- which brings high carbon dioxide emissions -- or natural gas from Russia, supplies of which are not yet secured.
"If we can only get natural gas from Russia, then the price will be high," she said, arguing that opening the nuclear option would at least improve the Finns' negotiating position.

Opinions on more nuclear power vary across the trade union spectrum, with unions some hotly opposed. Officials deny there could be any link between a bid to open the nuclear debate and labour market support for Finland joining EMU.
But privately, an economist close to heavy industry unions said: "That kind of link ... is completely logical from our point of view."
He welcomed Niinisto's remarks, seeing them as an opening shot which would lead Lipponen's government to break its pledge and debate the nuclear option "before midsummer".
